speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-FAILURE TO CO-ORDINATE REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT POLICIES AND TO REFER ISSUE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government's failure to co-ordinate its regional development policies under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion with other government activities, and its failure to bring in an appropriate reference to place this issue before the Standing Committee on Regional Development.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, this motion is
brought forward today out of the sense of frustration that we have experienced since this session started; first, our frustration in trying to receive information from the government regarding their regional development policies and regarding the various development programs that are in operation under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and second, our utter frustration over our unsuccessful attempts to have a meeting of the Standing Committee on Regional Development convened.

Notwithstanding the fact that we are now well into the session, and that the members of the Standing Committee on Regional Development, which is supposedly the committee of this House charged with the responsibilities that come under the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand), have been appointed since the first day of the session, the government-and we can only believe it is the government that has this responsibility-has failed to convene an organizational meeting of this committee for the purpose of electing a chairman and a vice chairman. As a consequence of that, we have been frustrated in our attempts to bring before Parliament what we feel to be one of the most serious problems facing the country today, namely that of regional development, and also what we believe to be the government's failure to this date to deal with that problem adequately. So, we use this device in the hope that perhaps the minister, whom I am glad to see in his place and whom I hope to see on his feet today, will get the message from what I have to say and from the remarks of other hon. members during the course of this debate.
The aim of regional development is not a new one to this country. As a matter of fact, it is as old as confederation, but certainly since that time we have had a series of new programs. We have had revised programs and replaced programs, all supposedly to be the panacea to deal with the problem of regional development. But, Mr. Speaker, we still have regional disparities in this country. We still have the consequences of regional disparity notwithstanding grandiose attempts by the government and the minister, notwithstanding what has been said by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the promises he made to the country during the course of the last election campaign.
In 1961, we saw the beginning of the ARDA program, a program designed at that time to improve land use in the poorer rural areas of Canada, and hence designed to upgrade the economies of these areas. Then, in 1968 the original ARDA program was replaced by what became known as the FRED program, the Fund for Rural Economic Development, which was to provide money for other purposes as well as land use improvement, which was to provide for long-range planning of rural development, with consultation to take place between the federal and provincial governments. We know what happened to poor FRED. Poor FRED is dead.
February 3, 1970

In the meantime, the Area Development Incentives Program was begun with a view to encouraging industrial development. Under this program, started with such great promise in 1963, special areas were designated because of their high levels of unemployment, and firms willing to establish in these special areas were given concessions or grants by the government. We all know what happened to ADIA.
These were the national programs, but there were also special programs such as the Atlantic Development Board, which was started in 1962 and which recognized the special needs of the area known as the Atlantic provinces. In its short history, the Atlantic Development Board certainly fulfilled many of its expectations. It did great things in the four Atlantic provinces. It took on the responsibility for the over-all economic development in the region and for the stimulation of new regional programs. It made special aid available to the provinces for highway construction and for power development, all designed to make this traditionally backward area of the country more attractive to industry. Mr. Speaker, we know what happened to the Atlantic Development Board.
By 1968 we had a hodgepodge of government programs, some of them in conflict with the others, all with the general aim of improving the poorer regions of the country, but we had little or no co-ordination between them. For example, ARDA was first administered by the Department of Agriculture and then it went to the Department of Forestry. The Area Development Agency, which was responsible for industrial incentives, was under the Department of Industry. The Atlantic Development Board passed through different hands several times.
The result was administrative chaos. But also the result was one of continuing hardship for the people of the regionally disadvantaged areas who had been led to believe, by the introduction of these programs, that a new day had arrived. The promise of these various programs, which are now supposed to be coordinated under the minister, has never been fulfilled, perhaps with the exception of the Atlantic Development Board and it died before it had a chance to implement its program fully.
By the summer of 1969 it was obvious that something would have to be done to bring some order into the whole area. Now, we have the new Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which brings together all of 21611-591

these various programs dealing with regional disparity, and indeed which is charged by Parliament with co-ordinating them.
The minister in charge of this department-this point was made during the course of the debate setting up the department, and it is well to repeat it now-was vested by Parliament with enormous powers, powers that in my view no other minister of the Crown has ever had in peacetime. He was authorized, on his own initiative and on his own authority, to designate areas which he felt were in need of special assistance to improve the economic opportunities of their residents. He could virtually do anything which he felt would improve the economic conditions within these areas. He could make grants to provincial governments. He could make provision whereby provincial services could be expanded. He could make loans. He could even make outright grants to firms planning to locate in the areas. He could secure the co-operation of a special body to undertake development projects in an area. Hon. members who follow me in this debate will be making special reference to what has been taking place in the province of Prince Edward Island since the minister became responsible for regional development.
But more important, Mr. Speaker, the minister was supposed to co-ordinate all the programs of all of the other federal departments which would have some influence on the area of regional development and regional incentives. Those of us who had doubts about the advisability of Parliament granting such vast power to one minister could draw some consolation from the thought that the minister was genuine and enthusiastic in his intent. Consequently, we could expect that the power which Parliament had entrusted to him would be used in a very fast and very dramatic way, and that by virtue of these powers he would be able to deal with some of the glaring examples of regional disparity without going through a great deal of bureaucratic red tape. That is what Parliament intended at that time.
Unhappily for us, and in particular more unhappily for those people who live in the regionally disadvantaged areas, we now have the feeling that all isn't well with the government's regional development efforts.

governments? Because of the provincial consultations, the minister said, the government cannot discuss why some areas, such as Cornwall for example, are not designated despite evident and pressing need.

The deputy minister, Mr. Kent, is sent to these consultations, but no communiques are issued, no reports are made and the House is not informed. The ministers return to Ottawa and do what they decided to do before they left for these consultations. This is this government's operational definition of participatory democracy. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate, may I say that I welcome the opportunity that has been afforded us by the motion proposed by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) to deal with this entire subject. The members of this party have been as frustrated as the hon. member for St. John's East has been in trying to obtain information about the government's regional development program. We have been frustrated also because of the failure to convene a meeting of the regional development committee. This failure, I think, reflects on the government.
Just before ending his remarks, the hon. member for St. John's East said that the minister does not want the committee to travel around the country, and to eastern Quebec and the Maritimes in particular, because it will discover how little has been done. I am very happy he alluded to that situation. I, and other members of my party, will mention a number of areas of endeavour that we think should receive immediate priority and consideration from the government. Regional development, since the 1968 federal election, should have been an aspect of government activity meriting high priority. Many people in this country were happy to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) say during his election campaign that as soon as possible economic disparities, regional disparities and economic inequities existing in this country would be removed and corrected. Those people were sadly disappointed because so little has been done. It appears to me that little is being planned for the future in this area.
You know, Mr. Speaker, in the last year and a half we have heard much about problems of Canadian unity, separatism and alienation. There is real talk of separatism. In western Canada, people who feel alienated from the central government in Ottawa are beginning to talk of separating. The main reason for their attitude in my opinion is economic alienation, the alienation of these people from the mainstream of Canadian life. Many of these people are unemployed or working for wages which are insufficient to support the standard they are entitled to in a country as rich as Canada. These people are frustrated. Unless we bring about social and economic changes in many regions of Canada
February 3, 1970

suffering from inequities and unless all regions of Canada can be equal partners in confederation, no one can say that this country will stay together for the next 100 years.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Our party has long said that present regional inequities in Canada are intolerable and that we must upgrade the living standards of the people of some regions. Since the 1920's, the gap between the "haves" and "have-nots" in Canada has not narrowed. This cannot be tolerated in a country with the riches and know-how we have. We cannot afford to perpetuate the differences of wealth existing in various regions of the country and the situation in which a man's fate or income is determined more on the basis of where he lives than on the basis of his ambition or ability. Often the region in which he lives is a very dominant factor in deciding his opportunities for employment, the kind of education his children will receive and the future of his family. There are many examples of this. What is the result? The result is that the skills of many Canadians are not developed. In many cases, the skills they do have are not used to their fullest potential. These people do not have an opportunity to explore to the fullest what they wish to explore and to do what they wish to do.
Speaking in harsh economic terms, this lack of development is very costly to the country as a whole. According to economic predictions, hundreds of millions of dollars are lost every year because people are not given the opportunities they would like to have in various regions of the country. Underdeveloped regions of Canada are caught in a vicious circle. I am sure many members who speak this afternoon will mention many of these facts. We see that the underdeveloped and depressed regions are suffering from low incomes, unemployment and a low amount of capital to create new jobs. As a result, there is low productivity in these areas. This leads to a lower level of education, poor health and welfare services and a lower standard of living.
There are many ramifications to this problem. This is another reason why we cannot sit back. We must start exploring and initiating new ideas and programs in the whole area of regional economic development. In my own province of Saskatchewan, many of these things are very true. I know that there is a continual migration of young people from the rural areas to the cities, as well as
Regional Development
from the poorer areas to the richer areas of Canada. These are the areas in which there are opportunities for people with skills and university educations. This only complicates and worsens conditions in some of the economically depressed areas of Canada.
Last year, the Economic Council of Canada presented its fifth annual review. It dealt with poverty in this country and I think opened the eyes of many people to the fact that there was poverty in Canada and that something had to be done about it. I wish to read a short extract from the report of the Economic Council on the problem of poverty:
Poverty in Canada is real. Its numbers are not in the thousands, but millions. There is more of it than our society can tolerate, more than our economy can afford, and far more than existing measures and efforts can cope with. Its persistence, at a time when the bulk of Canadians enjoy one of the highest standards of living in the world, is a disgrace.
We must realize the significance of this poverty both in rural and urban Canada. I do not want to suggest that the Department of Regional, Economic Expansion is the only government department that should be fighting poverty. It isn't. Poverty is a many-headed beast. It must be attacked from many different directions. The Department of Manpower and Immigration and the Department of National Health and Welfare also play a part. However, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and its minister are among the key people in the fight against poverty.
In 1967 the Dominion Bureau of Statistics said that approximately 45 per cent of Canadian families with incomes falling beneath the low income lines lived in nonurban areas. This income line was determined by the Economic Council of Canada. We know that the incidence of poverty is much higher in areas such as the Maritimes, eastern Quebec and indeed in the Prairies. It is also much higher among our Indian, Metis and Eskimo population. This is a problem which the committee responsible for this department should discuss here and now. We cannot continue procrastinating. If we do, the problem will become more and more complicated and more difficult to solve.
I have mentioned some areas and groups where the incidence of poverty is very high, but they are not the only areas. It is also very high among the white population in the big cities. The Economic Council of Canada said that perhaps one-third to one-half of the poverty in Canada today exists in the big cities of this country. This has very many serious

February 3, 1970
Regional Development
complications and ramifications. It is not a simple problem of income distribution. It is not a simple, economic problem. It has many side effects, one of which is a sense of helplessness and alienation for these people from the society in which they live. There is a culture of poverty. It is a never ending circle in which many people are trapped, creating many social and economic problems. I will give an example of this.
In the United States, a commission was set up to study the unrest, violence and alienation in many of the big cities in that country. They said that one of the reasons for this was poverty and that there was a very high correlation between poverty and crime. This is not very surprising because many of these people are put in situations that are vastly different from those of the majority of the people in that country. Some of these people have to resort to crime because of necessity, because they are alienated from the society in which they live or because of bitterness. These are things which we must also face up to in this country and which will have to be faced very soon by this government.
When John F. Kennedy was President of the United States, a commission was established to investigate much of the unrest in the big cities. They found that one reason was that people were leaving the rural areas of the United States, the farms, towns and villages, and moving into the cities. They were unskilled, in a strange atmosphere and became completely lost and alienated in this atmosphere. They were the rural poor and became the urban poor. This is why we must be concerned with these people now living in the rural and urban areas of our country. This is where the Department of Regional Economic Expansion must start to work immediately. Often, it is difficult to readily detect many of the poor people in this country. We must bear in mind that collectively the poor people are quite inarticulate. They are not organized and to a large extent are voiceless. They do not have a Chamber of Commerce, Bar Association or union to speak for them, to outline their conditions and particular circumstances. This is one reason why, for so many years, these problems have been overlooked. Another reason is that we have been too content to file these problems away under different headings in the various departments of government.
The poor people of this country need to have something done for them soon. This government will have to react because the pover-

ty in this country is very great. It is a great problem to the individual. This is my greatest concern because the individual is being condemned to a life of low income, a life that does not give him or his family an opportunity to do what he wishes. He is sometimes victimized by the lack of proper medical attention or care. He does not have the employment or educational opportunities and often finds himself in a way of life where he does not seem to have a sense of purpose or does not seem to know what he should be doing. These are matters that must be studied. These problems must be solved.
Poverty is also very costly to our society. Every year it costs this country hundreds of millions of dollars because the poor people are held back and are not allowed to do what they want to do. I wish to quote a very short paragraph from an article that appeared in the Ottawa Citizen on November 11, 1969. It reads:
Poverty may have cost the country as much as $2,284,600,000 in 1961 in loss of output that would otherwise have been achieved if the poor had been properly employed, says an analysis of census figures.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
This is just one indication that if we fail to act now, society as a whole will suffer. As I said earlier, this is not my main concern-my concern is principally for the people who live in poverty.
There are one or two other things I might say on this subject, but my time is limited and some of my hon. friends will be bringing out a variety of other points. However, in closing, I do wish to mention one other matter which is of great concern to me and to many hon. members from western Canada in all political parties. When the government announced last summer the areas to be designated under the new Area Development Incentives Act, I was unhappy to note that only a small area of Saskatchewan was included under the plan. We all know about the economic crisis which presently exists in Saskatchewan. Without going into details, let me say that it affects not only farmers but small businessmen and working people alike.
I should like the minister to explain, when he arises to make a statement in the House, why most of Saskatchewan has been excluded, in the main, from the benefits of this legislation. I would suggest to him that because of the present crisis the whole of the province should be designated as a special area, having regard to the economic situation
February 3, 1970

which confronts almost all of the people in that province. In the circumstances, I ask the minister to seriously consider including all of Saskatchewan as a designated area.
Before I sit down, I wish to move an amendment to the motion which is before us today; I hope it will enable us to bring out a few more points. It is seconded by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and it reads as follows:
That the motion be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"and this House further condemns the government for its failure to lessen regional poverty across Canada, and for its failure to create job opportunities so sorely needed at this time."

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-FAILURE TO CO-ORDINATE REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT POLICIES AND TO REFER ISSUE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was in Quebec city yesterday for the meeting of Finance ministers and I learned that a debate would take place today on regional development. Even though it meant altering my schedule, I was most happy to do it, because that debate was to give me the opportunity to rise in the House and deal with an extremely complex problem affecting a great number of Canadians. I also thought that it would at least lead the spokesmen for opposition parties not only to express their views but also to give us food for thought on regional development.
Even though I have clear ideas on a professional and moral basis, I do not doubt that there is a way to improve the tools we have given ourselves. I already notice loopholes in pieces of legislation passed hardly a few months ago. It was rather logical for me to expect, especially from the spokesman for the official opposition, a comprehensive study of the whole philosophy of regional development and not merely meaningless and unproductive generalizations. And such was the substance of the remarks made by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). I have been trying to remember some meaningful point of his speech, which I unfortunately cannot do, 21611-60
Regional Development
because there is none. It was a general lament about unemployment and the alleged secrecy shrouding the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
It is certainly difficult to eliminate regional disparities in Canada. As the hon. member for St. John's East mentioned, probably as far back as the time of Confederation governments have been trying to wipe them out, but with little success. The only success worth mentioning is that, had we not implemented some of the programs, the gap would perhaps be wider still than it is now. But this is only an assumption, and I do not want to rest my argument on it.
At any rate, it is obvious that we have failed to bridge this gap. Through legislation passed last year, we have tried to give ourselves efficient tools which might enable us to reduce considerably these disparities. While we are attempting to make them disappear, there are things happening at the economic level which affect the implementation of our programs.
In a country as diversified as ours, where there are flagrant contradictions in the field of economics, how is it possible to reach the aims we have set for ourselves? For instance, how do we go about priming the economy in underdeveloped regions while some areas of the country are battling with inflation and others fighting recession? What monetary policy should we adopt? What kind of fiscal policy should we advocate to help certain regions without further aggravating inflation in others? The hon. member for St. John's East could have told us which monetary policy would allow us to reach that goal. It may be that opposition members have excellent ideas which they could share with us.
In our opinion, there are but two possible solutions to our problems: an anti-inflationary policy has to be adopted in an effort to curb the inflationary trend in some regions of the country, and a development policy has to be implemented in the underdeveloped areas.
These are two different policies and we believe it is the only way to reach our objectives. In fact, when inflation pushes prices up in Ontario, Alberta or British Columbia, we realize as well as anyone else that they also climb in St. John's, Moncton, Quebec City and everywhere. If we have to apply a restrictive monetary policy to combat inflation, we notice that such a policy brings adverse consequences on the under-developed areas where a more liberal monetary policy would

February 3, 1970
Regional Development
be called for. This renders the problem much more acute than it would normally be.
We have developed a new policy which implies a considerable increase of industrial incentives in order to persuade business to establish in less developed areas. What was the result? So far, 544 applications made to the department under the new legislation have been approved by the minister. Comparing the impact of the new legislation with what happened when the Area Development Incentives Act was passed in 1965, we see that the first application made after the law came into force was approved in January 1966. This year, in the same month, close to 80 applications had been approved.
When the legislation was passed in July or August last, the department was ready to operate though, of course, it was necessary to proceed to such adjustments as, for instance, training personnel. Some think that it is easy to find the required personnel in order to promote industrial development or to conclude with provinces agreements relating to regional development. Let those who claim they can train personnel more quickly tell us how they do it. As to ourselves, we had, first of all, to find the necessary personnel and it is what we did.
Moreover, negotiations had to be conducted with the provinces as regards regional development, which brought into play what we call infrastructures.
The hon. member for St. John's East asks us: where are the jobs that have been created? That is a very well-timed question, because in fact, there is more unemployment than before. A very pertinent question indeed! He should have given us the answer himself, because this is not only a group of irresponsible people that we have here. Everyone knows that when the department approves an application for some industrial incentive, two years, on the average, are needed before the firm is established and in a position to hire workers.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

structure on their own. Therefore we take money from people in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia and other prosperous provinces and give it to provinces or municipalities that need it.
It is our duty to see to it that the projects submitted are rational and intended to reach the objectives on which we have set our sight. It takes a while to read agreements with the provinces, Mr. Speaker, it cannot be done overnight. Indeed, it supposes several meetings. We have set a target date, next April 1st, to start spending money in that field. I have every reason to believe that we will do so in just about every province in Canada. Agreements are being reached in almost every area. In a few places, there are still a few details to straighten out. But I wonder why the commotion because it took us a few months to sign agreements that are extremely complex and difficult, because we did not report to the House every day or every week on those agreements. How can you negotiate an agreement publicly? We are negotiating agreements dealing with objectives and matters of provincial jurisdiction.
We would like the province to agree before we announce what the agreement is all about. It seems to me there is nothing shocking about the way we proceed and hon. members will get an opportunity to know about all the agreements negotiated with the provinces.
Why such secrecy? Precisely because the agreements deal with matters of provincial jurisdiction. We have no jurisdiction when it comes to sewage systems, roads, education or hospitals. We have to negotiate with the provinces and try to establish priorities in agreement with them.
What is shocking about that? The hon. member for St. John's East would probably want me to say: Well, here is what we suggest, what the province puts forward, what Mr. So-and-so says. Who will venture to imagine that it is possible to negotiate in this way? It is impossible. Once an agreement is reached, nothing prevents hon. members to criticize and to tell us that we went too far or not far enough. This is quite a normal process and I think that we can then arrive at constructive criticism. But simply to suggest to the public that we did not keep them informed about the various stages of our negotiations with the provinces, this is really childish.
I will deal now with the matter of co-ordination of activities. We know that the work which is carried out by the provinces and the

municipalities, by degree of importance, is fairly more significant than that carried out by the federal government itself and that is why there must be some co-ordination within the federal government of course, but most of all between the agencies of the various levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal, and that is our obvious purpose when negotiating agreements.

This is not a problem particular to Canada; it is also an American problem and one that plagues the western world, it may also be a world evil. It is probably most legitimate to require more efforts on our part in that field but there again, it might be a great, general, and even generous idea but it does not give a specific answer to the current problems.
The overall proposal made by the opposition, betrays their ignorance of the whole matter and also indicates a lack of courage. When you want to come to grips with a policy, you have to identify it and point at is weaknesses and failures. Those responsible for it must be brought back to their senses. All they can do is to use one big word: "coordination". This leads nowhere. It simply gives some hon. member a chance to take the floor for half an hour.
This question is of paramount importance for the future of Canada, and it should be a matter of concern for us. All they can find to say, however, is that there is a lack of coordination, putting the blame on the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister started off by describing the remarks of the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) as banal, general and insipid. I would have to say it is a long time since I heard such a banal defence of a program as that given by the minister, but I would not describe the minister's speech as insipid because obviously he tried to make up in heat what he failed to generate by way of light.
I am very concerned about the lack of a program generally with regard to this question of regional economic expansion. We supported the creation of the department. We co-operated in getting the measure through the House, although it was not the way we would have proceeded ourselves. Nevertheless, we wanted to give the government every opportunity to develop a plan of operation. But the fact is that nothing of substance has yet come from the minister or the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Meanwhile a good many regions of the country are

February 3, 1970
Regional Development
losing ground economically vis-a-vis the rest of the country.
I wish to say to the minister on behalf of myself, the members of my party, and I am sure the country as a whole, that the honeymoon is over for the minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with regard to the question of regional disparities. It is time that the minister really told the country what he and his department are doing, and it is time the government permitted the committee concerned to examine in a reasonable way the program of the government with regard to regional disparities. I do not mean a rushed job when the estimates are before the Committee. It is impossible for the minister and the government to justify their refusal to allow the appropriate committee to examine the minister's program. It throws suspicion on the whole approach of the government.
It is two years since the election, but the department has done so little and the govern-iment as a whole has done so little, that they will not permit the committee to examine what has been done. Sure, there have been some grants made in some of the provinces, but nothing very much in others.
The minister pleads that he needs time. He says he could not create jobs tomorrow. Yet he did not attempt to deny that disparity is deepening in the country and is spreading in the country. For example, consider the position of the province of Saskatchewan. Two or three years ago this province became qualified as a have rather than a have-not province and yet the provisions for equalization payments to it were eliminated. Consider the situation in that province today, and the help and positive measures being given and taken by the federal government with regard to it.
Saskatchewan has reached the point where its premier had to beg the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) not to smile when he was discussing its problems. The federal government cannot claim that it has even started any program there. I do not think the minister would even pretend that he had done anything, and we are not aware of any measures undertaken by the Department of Industry or any other department. The government is displaying a cold-blooded, disinterested attitude toward the problems of that province, and it is not much wonder that there is a certain amount of talk about western separatism.
As far as I can see, the minister and the government have written off the whole idea of developing the near north, and are appar-

ently content to leave it flounder as best it can. Parliament has given this minister extraordinary powers so far as his own department is concerned, but the only way these powers have been used so far has been to put a strangle hold on the province of Prince Edward Island.
The federal government claims to be making a contribution of $225 million under the plan agreed with Prince Edward Island, but that is very misleading, Mr. Speaker. There is no such contribution over a period of 15 years so far as new federal money is concerned. A good deal of that amount is made up of bookkeeping transfers, as well as the phasing out and consolidation of existing programs. I would estimate that not more than $60 million at most of this alleged $225 million is new federal money going into Prince Edward Island over a period of 15 years.
There is also the danger that the federal government will not extend new programs as they arise to Prince Edward Island, with the excuse that Prince Edward Island is covered by a plan of its own. We had the announcement last spring that $6 million would be granted for highway projects to the Atlantic provinces, but none of this was to be allotted to Prince Edward Island on the ground that other arrangements had been made under its plan. How realistic is it to expect the province of P.E.I. to put up something like $500 million over a period of 15 years? I hope the plan will produce dynamic growth on that island so that it can meet that commitment, but I am very suspicious of any federal government that would put such a price tag as that on Prince Edward Island's entry into the plan.
I am concerned that the federal government is looking forward, if it is not already doing so, to running P.E.I. like a piece of federal property. I say that no federal plan, department or government should deprive the people of that province of their right to selfgovernment. The plan now in operation for Prince Edward Island is extremely centralized. Every decision is centralized here in Ottawa. Whatever degree of decentralization there used to be under the Atlantic Development Board has been removed, and everything is concentrated here in Ottawa. We have to ask, what are the minister and his colleagues up to?
Certainly, the policies of the federal government are placing very heavy financial pressures on all of the eastern provinces. We must recognize, as the Economic Council has point-
February 3, 1970

ed out time and time again, the importance of all these provinces being able to render a satisfactory degree of services, particularly growth related services, if they are ever to overcome the problems of economic disparity. Yet three of these five provinces have not yet been able to bring in the medicare plan, a nationwide program, although I believe that two at least are committed to doing so. The federal government must recognize the financial problems in all of these provinces which are suffering economic disparity, yet it seems to me it is exerting constant financial pressure on them and refusing to recognize their financial difficulties in providing services in any effective way. The minister made a great play about asking how one would apply a monetary policy in an effective way. Well, he could at least try. I would like to try. And what about fiscal policy? I say to the minister that the government has not made the slightest effort to adjust its fiscal policy to these areas. The whole effect of its fiscal policy down there has been to cut back and to aggravate the problems of slow growth. It is essential that these provinces be able to provide these services in order to participate in development programs, but as far as I can see the whole tendency, if not the intent, of the present policies of the government is to grind down these provinces.
The tax structure committee forecast the rapidity of the growth and the financial needs of the provinces for basic government services, yet no recognition has been given to that. As far as I can see, after using an antiinflation program as an excuse, and perhaps using negotiated plans as the implement, the tendency if not the intent of the federal government seems to be to bring all of these provinces into a condition of financial subserviency to the federal government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-FAILURE TO CO-ORDINATE REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT POLICIES AND TO REFER ISSUE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when some hon. members opposite were still in the childhood stage I sat in the gallery of the other place and watched when the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada were signed. It was a very unhappy incident for me, as I had opposed the idea of Newfoundland entering the Canadian confederation. I suppose most of my motivation at that time was emotional, although a bit of logic did creep into the various arguments. At one stage most of the comments that I made publicly on the subject were based on the standard complaint that I have been hearing for many years from such provinces as New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, the basic argument being that confederation was a bit of an abortion, both geographically and economically, and that Newfoundland would be a dory tied on to the schooner.
I made my decision very early following confederation that if we were to be Canadians, despite my best judgment of those days, then we ought to be good Canadians. Over the last 21 years both in public life and before, I have commented upon and tried to find solutions for and make recommendations about, so-called regional economic disparity. Of course, we did not call it that in the early days. I do not know what word was used but

February 3, 1970
Regional Development
there was generally a feeling on the part of those living in Newfoundland, and probably those in the Atlantic provinces as well, that in some way or other we were not getting our just dues, as it were, out of the promise of confederation. In 100 years we had not been able to achieve the general objectives, the promises, that seemed to be implicit in the original concept of one nation from sea to sea. I have to say, however, that over that period of 21 years I am satisfied that my own province has probably gone ahead more than it would have under any other arrangement. But I am also compelled to say that most of the progress and gains made were obvious for the simple reason that for such a long period there had been relatively little progress that what we gained seemed like a great deal. I suppose what it amounted to was that half a loaf appeared as good as a full one, and certainly better than no bread at all.
Today, as I strenuously grapple with this problem of regional economic expansion, I am conscious that the basic difficulty is the same as it was 21 years ago. It has been compounded, complicated by developments that have taken place, but the basic problem remains. I do not know the degree to which it is common to all four provinces, but in Newfoundland it seems to be a matter of trying to find sufficient gainful employment for a growing population. One of the miracles of confederation as far as Newfoundland is concerned is that we have managed, despite a decline in one end of the scale, to keep our population moving up slightly. We have not had the massive exodus that many people, including myself, forecast once the immigration barriers between Newfoundland and Canada were removed. Even though we have been able to keep the population static, the fact of the matter is that job opportunities simply are not there.
To hon. members opposite who are critical of this program I would say that, while I share their frustration and concern, I believe that if we were to announce tomorrow more attractive incentives than those the minister has outlined, which must rank with the most attractive in any western country, it still would be very very difficult to find people prepared to introduce the kind of industrial development necessary to take care of those now unemployed. As well as this group, there are others coming along at an ever-increasing rate, that is assuming our population will remain at the level it is now and that we have the normal increase.
When the minister spoke about the number of jobs the program has generated I have no quarrel with the figures. I can see some evidence already of the effect of the incentives program in Newfoundland. A week ago today, I was present at the opening of a new fishing installation which will give employment to many people. The cost is in the neighbourhood of $21 million, of which the federal government's contribution was substantially more than one-third; but this is really still only a drop in the bucket.
Perhaps the hon. Leader of the Opposition is right when he says that only if we can get together in terms of a committee discussion will these problems disappear. But I suggest in all honesty that as the former leader of a Conservative government in the province of Nova Scotia, he knows that it is not as simple as that. In fact, we are going to have an extremely difficult job even with incentives, even with growth centres and the like, to provide the kind of employment and the levels of employment which are necessary.
It is because of this complexity and because the history of the last 21 years has shown that many of the programs have not been successful that I do not criticize the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand) for what hon. members opposite referred to as his slowness in moving. Rather, I commend him for having the good sense to make sure that this time we have covered as many bases as possible. We do not want to go off in all directions and then find, ten years from now, that we have not achieved very much.
Hon. members from Newfoundland should be the last to suggest that there should be some sort of a precipitate haste in setting up industrial enterprises of any kind. We really must be sure that we have the right answers.
The fisheries, of course, are still pretty basic in terms of our Newfoundland economy. About a year or so ago we had a situation which all of us agreed was desperate. As a result of actions which were taken there has been a remarkable transition. The fact of the matter is that the fresh frozen fish industry is in an extremely buoyant state now and looking better all the time. I have heard repeatedly, when travelling to Newfoundland and other parts of the Maritime provinces, that the only answer to providing quick relief to economically depressed areas on the coast is "Give us another fish plant".
There is an awful parallel, and it is terribly striking, to what was said a few years ago to our wheat farmers on the prairies. It will be remembered that they were told to grow all the wheat they could because everything looked great. Let us not fall into that pitfall, and there is a great danger here.
There is a second danger when it comes to providing incentives in the fishing industry and that is,-I believe the hon. member who is the spokesman for the official opposition might be inclined to agree-in moving into the herring fishery simply because there is a market and providing fishermen with the means of getting into it. Again we would be, to use a familiar old expression, killing the goose that lays the golden eggs. There is a limit to the amount of job creation that can be performed within the fishing industry of the Atlantic provinces, and this is basic to the whole object of regional economic expansion.
These fisheries problems are related to something else about which hon. members in opposition will have to make up their minds. I do not blame them for their difficulty in doing so, but I say that the issue of centralization, in one form or another, must be decided one way or another. If we are to help people in the fishing industry in the small communities around the coast of Newfoundland, and I am confining myself to that area
Regional Development because it is the one I know best, if we are to provide those people with the kind of future they have a right to expect, if they are to realize the full promise of confederation, as I have called it, then we cannot do it in many of these smaller places without moving the people out. So, the growth centre concept to which the minister has referred and on which, as I happen to know, he and his officials have worked extremely hard in recent months, is a very valid one. But it contains difficulties as well. I can see that when a designation is made hon. gentlemen opposite will look at it and say, "Why is it in this area; why is it not somewhere else?" Inevitably, naturally, understandably and defensively hon. gentlemen are going to say, "But there is not enough in my riding to be of special interest."
What is the alternative? If you are not going to have development areas, if you are not to have growth centres or points round which you can polarize the population and try to provide employment opportunities for them, the answer is that we shall have to continue with what I have called the pastoral syndrome in Newfoundland. I suggest that many people think of that as the easiest way out. It is very easy, when one goes into a community or some backwood area of Newfoundland, to say, "We could not agree more; you are entitled to all the services and to all the improvements that you like."
But surely to goodness, if we are to take any real interest in these people we have to try at least to help them by getting them to move to growth centres and there provide employment for them. I know the stock answer to that is that we have put the cart before the horse and, in some respects, we probably did. Centralization may have moved ahead faster than was wise in some circumstances because, and I agree with those hon. members who have levelled this criticism at us, those who moved in did not have jobs. And if they do not have jobs where they are now, let us also remember that they would not have had jobs if they had remained behind either. So, I say that centralization in some form has to be part of the development program.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, back in the old days before the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) kidnapped the Liberal government and transformed it into his own image, in the days when the present Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) and the present Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) were still private citizens in Quebec being ardently wooed by the Liberal hierarchy, these men were commonly referred to as the three wise men. I have not heard this expression used very frequently in recent times. As a matter of fact, recent events have somewhat obliterated this myth. The three wise men have now been supplemented by another trio to which I will refer as the three blind mice. These men, 1 suggest, are the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen).
The reason I make this assertion is that I believe these three individuals are blind to Canada's regional difficulties. They are either too obsessed with their positions or too timid to grapple with the problems that confront them. This failure to promote effective action to overcome problems of regional disparity is serious in all parts of the country and very much so in western Canada.
Not only has the government's consistent and obvious disinterest in the west bred a feeling of isolation from the rest of Canada,
February 3, 1970

February 3, 1970
Regional Development returns. In the face of such figures, it is difficult for a western Canadian to understand why he is almost totally ignored by Ottawa, except when taxes are levied, and why common sense and common justice do not compel this government to stop making empty promises and start acting.
It is particularly difficult to understand why the west has been excluded from assistance by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. The boundaries of his designated area were set arbitrarily by himself and his officials and from what I can see, with no set of rules or universal criteria. The minister claims the provinces were consulted fully before the lines were drawn, but this is at variance with what is claimed by provincial authorities, particularly the premier of my own province.
There was an exchange of letters last year between myself and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. In a letter addressed to me dated October 10 last, the minister said:
Our conclusion, after consultation with the provincial government, (that is the government of Alberta), was that the program would produce the greatest benefits for the province as a whole if the southern region was designated.
My information is that the minister consulted no one in Alberta except his colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, who just happened to represent a riding that coincided roughly with the designated area. In another part of the same letter, the minister stated:

We are talking about the kind of program that my department can best employ to ease the necessary adjustment process and cushion its effects on the people of the prairies.
At that time he said he was negotiating with the provincial government about instituting such a program. This is as far back as October 10. But no one has heard a word about the program since, or seen any sign of one being initiated. This is the type of windy delusion which comes from the offices of the trio to which I have referred- pronouncements which have led westerners to doubt the integrity of this government and to lose faith in the viability of Canada under such management.
It is more than a co-incidence that the minister has consistently refused to table in this House copies of the letters he claims were exchanged between him and various western premiers on the topic I have just been discussing. Reference to questions 581 and 582 will indicate this clearly.

Another glaring example of injustice and a further ground for the build-up of western animosity is to be found in the government's dairy policy. The government now proposes a $10 million cut in funds available under the Canadian dairy policy on the professed ground of aiding its austerity drive. What will happen, in fact, is that the share of western dairy farmers will be reduced in proportion to that of the central region. It is true there is over-production in Canada's dairy industry- but it is not in the west. The over-production happens to be in Quebec, but this fact is ignored. The committee is being asked to develop a national policy, the results of which will simply penalize those regions which have exercised a discretion in the field of supply management, and have not significantly overproduced. There is little use in prolonging this recital of the many shortcomings of the government's regional economic expansion and agriculture policies. They are so blatant that we can all see them.
I turn, now, to the third element in the trio of departments which the Minister of Agriculture claimed would solve the problems of the west. I listened with interest the other day to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration making much of little in his announcement of that department's success in finding jobs for students. As far as I and others are concerned, they were mere empty boasts. Let me cite only one case, that of a graduate student for whom no job can be found. This young man is now being badgered by solicitors for repayment of a student loan. He is Mr. Kenneth R. Powley of Vegre-ville, Alberta, an architect who graduated in June of 1968 but could find only fleeting employment until January 1969, and none since. He visited the nearest manpower centre seeking assistance, and according to a letter I received from the Minister of Manpower last September, he registered for employment with the manpower centre at Edmonton shortly after his graduation in 1968.
To date, the result has been nil. He is still unemployed, and I have a sheaf of application letters to show that it is not for lack of trying to get a job. He is willing to work in practically any field and at any location. Yet this great department, with its policy of job mobility, has totally failed to assist him. The case of Mr. Powley symbolizes the current condition of the west. He is a victim of federal promises which are without substance or good faith. He is a symbol of the utter and complete failure of the government's promise of regional assistance through a combination
February 3, 1970

of the three departments most closely concerned. Had he lived elsewhere he might have been more fortunate.
These are some of the feelings of westerners which have been communicated to me in my travels. It is a combination of such inequities with little promise of hope which has created the prevailing hostility toward the federal government and a growing sense of alienation. The result has spurred discussion of separatism, talk of forming a regional power bloc and of possible union with the United States. In the interest of preserving Canada, the reversal of this trend must be considered a basic priority of the government. I firmly believe that if the present callous disregard of the west continues we, as Canadians, will all suffer the consequences.

As the motion presented by the hon. member for St. John's East has no meaning, it is very difficult to address oneself to it in an intelligent manner. It is a skeleton, some sort of noble cause without a defending knight. Mr. Speaker, the opposition motion presented today reads as follows:

That this House condemns the government's failure to co-ordinate its regional development policies under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion with other government activities, and its failure to bring in an appropriate reference to place this issue before the Standing Committee on Regional Development.

I intend first of all to let you know what I think of the advisability of such a motion and I will afterwards comment on the general economic expansion policy of the government.
I have naturally no right to impute motives to the mover, but nevertheless, I can ask myself what he had in mind when he presented that motion. I think it is a weak motion, even from a strictly political point of view. We all know to what extent the hon. member is imbued with political motives. This motion-I cannot help saying it-is not worth a cent.
A motion of censure brought in against the government always contains a great many negative elements. It is normal, they say. But when they stoop to childish and silly things, we can wonder, and rightly so, if money put at the disposal of opposition members for research purposes is not a total loss. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the short time at my disposal this afternoon, and at the risk of being perhaps parochial, I should like to attempt to place on the record of this House as clearly and as

February 3, 1970
Regional Development succinctly as I possibly can the very serious situation which faces the government and the people of my province of Prince Edward Island. I do this in the hope that I may possibly foster a desire on the part of this government to do something immediately to relieve a very distressing problem. Action must be taken to reduce the growing gap between the rich and the poor provinces of Canada. Each region of this country must be accepted as an integral part of Canada and must be developed according to its special needs and according to its potential.
The reduction of the growing gap between the rich and the poor provinces is a national problem, and the major responsibility of solving it must rest with the federal government and no one else. I say that if the so-called just society is ever to be anything more than a flimsy and meaningless promise it must be based on the right of every citizen of this country, first of all, to acquire an adequate income and, second and just as important, to be able to enjoy the same essential public services as are being enjoyed by the people living in the so-called richer provinces. The federal government must be made to realize, as apparently it has not realized yet, that the major burden of financing regional growth in the poorer provinces is its responsibility. Why is it its responsibility? Primarily because money is necessary to do that job and the poorer provinces just do not have the money nor, unfortunately, do they have the opportunities now to raise the necessary money through taxation.
Let me return, if I may, to my own province. Under present conditions, how can the government of Prince Edward Island possibly raise more money through the medium of taxation? The average weekly wage of the worker in our province is $75.97-that is $38.06 a week below the national average. In November of 1969 our unemployment rate was 7.9 per cent of the labour force. At that time that was the highest of any province in Canada. We depend very heavily on agriculture, and yet more than one half of our island farmers gross less than $2,500 a year, before taking out their expenses. The situation is growing worse. For four consecutive years now, the capital investment in the province has been decreasing, and I suggest that we cannot have the base for levying taxes unless we have capital investment. Our business establishments are small-75 per cent of the firms in our province have sales of less than $5,000 a year.

Perhaps more serious than all of this is the fact that many of our young people who are just entering the productive year of their lives are leaving our province, and for good reason. They are leaving because they cannot find jobs there and wish to take advantage of the opportunities which are offered in the more rapidly growing regions in this country. I suggest that perhaps they cannot be blamed. When our province entered confederation in 1873, our population was 97,000 people. Today, 97 years later, the population is still only 110,000 people. That is an increase of
13,000	people in 97 years. Young people have to move out; there is just nothing there for them to do.
This migration is general all over the maritime provinces. In 1851, 22 per cent of all Canadians resided in the maritime provinces. In 1961, 11 per cent resided there. Unfortunately, these young men and women leave, as I said before, in the most productive years of their lives. We rear and educate them at a cost which is estimated to be $20,000 per child, and just as they reach the age at which they are able to contribute something to our economy they leave for Ontario or some other province in Canada or for a state in the United States where they can earn an adequate wage. Only 55 per cent of our population is in the age group of 15 to 64 years, that is the age when they are likely to be in the labour force and when they can make a valuable contribution to our economy. Our population, therefore, is made up of a disproportionate percentage of the very young and the very old and of course we know that the very young and the very old, instead of contributing to the economy of the province, are more inclined to draw out of it.
There must be a narrowing of the gap in personal income between our region and other regions of Canada, and this must be accomplished through the generation of income within the region. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the legislation to establish the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was introduced and debated in this House last summer, and when the principal item of legislation proposed by the department during that year-the Regional Development Incentives Act-was brought forward, I think it will be agreed that in all quarters of the House there was general agreement upon the need to develop an adequate regional development program and an adequate program of regional economic expansion.
While there were some points of disagreement on the specific aspects of the government's proposal, and in some cases serious disagreement in areas which members of this party felt could jeopardize the prospects for success of the program, I think there was general agreement upon the principle of developing such a program, and therefore agreement as to the principle of the legislation passed by this House. Thus it can be said, Mr. Speaker, that the government embarked upon this new program with a high degree of good will in all parts of the House and in Canada generally.
However, it seems to me that a good deal of this good will has been dissipated and washed away during the past several months as a result of some of the actions of the government, some of the things it has done and some of the things it has not done. No better example of the type of thing that has been done by the government can be found than the department's news release of last November 19. That news release issued by the department stated, "Regional program creating more new jobs." It went on to say:
The federal government's regional development program is creating new employment four times as fast as it did in 1968.
Then there was some elaboration on this matter. It was pointed out that from January to mid-November the department has

February 3, 1970
Regional Development approved 278 development incentives for firms intending to establish new plants or expand into slow growth regions of Canada. There were further details in the release about the estimated permanent employment which would result. There was also the statement that this activity was a good deal higher than in previous years.
It all sounded very fine, and consequently I asked for more information on this annouce-ment by the department. I moved a motion for papers in which 1 asked for a copy of the list of the 278 development incentive grants and for some other information. I was informed on January 28, Wednesday last, by the parliamentary secretary that "the cases referred to are not grants paid out but offers made." He went on to say, as reported at page 2928 of Hansard:
The details requested will be made public in all cases when the project is proceeded with, and before any grant is actually paid. But at the offer stage, confidentiality is essential to the program.
I want to make it clear that I am not blaming the department for bragging a little about getting a larger number of applications than in previous years, even though many of these applications would be from firms which were trying to get in under the deadline of the old legislation because in many cases they would not be able to qualify under the new legislation in view of the change of boundaries. I am not blaming the department for wanting to take a little credit for this. But it is clear from the answer given that these are not firm projects; there is nothing concrete about them.
They are only offers to the extent that the government is carrying out its commitment. They are only offers of grants if a decision is made by the private firm involved to proceed with the development project in question. Thus, it seems to me that the department's news release creates a false impression of what is being done under the aegis of this department.
It seems to me that there are a number of drastic failures and shortcoming in the government's program as it has developed up to the present time. The first major point is that the department has not developed an effective program that can be used as a weapon in the war on poverty. I think all hon. members will recognize that problems of poverty cannot and will not be solved overnight. I believe it must be said that to date we have not seen any evidence that the department is developing any sort of program that can really be

described as a attack on the whole problem of poverty. I do not intend to go into this matter in any further detail because the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) dealt with it in his address this afternoon.
The second point I wish to draw to the attention of the House is that the government has failed with its program in this department to counterbalance the impact of its policies of fiscal and monetary restraint in regions which are suffering economic setbacks or which are economically deprived and underdeveloped. Our attention has been drawn to the fact that the government will tolerate a high level of unemployment. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated that he is willing to tolerate a 6 per cent level of unemployment without any difficulty.
This means a 10 per cent rate of unemployment in Quebec, a 12 per cent rate in the Maritime provinces, and for my own province of Saskatchewan a 10 per cent rate of unemployment in the urban centres and communities. Thus, we see that the government's program in the area of regional economic expansion has not been effective and I suggest it will not be effective, within its present framework, in counterbalancing many of the ill-effects of the government's present program and policy of fiscal and monetary restraint.
Third, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that there has been political chicanery in the establishment of designated areas under the Regional Development Incentives Act. I have found it rather difficult to obtain answers and adequate information on government policy and approach in dealing with this particular matter. I have asked a good many questions on this subject during the current session of Parliament. One question I asked with respect to seven out of our ten provinces was the following:
What criteria were used by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in the selection of designated areas for the province-
The answer provided to each question was, "Weighted measures of rates of economic growth-employment, income and population-and of potential for secondary industry". This is a clear case, so far as I am concerned, of bureaucratic gobbledegook. Thus, we see what wording was used to set out the criteria for the designation of areas under this new legislation. Subsequently, I placed a motion for papers on the Order Paper asking for a copy of all correspondence between the gov-
February 3, 1970

ernment of Canada and each of the provinces regarding the selection of designated regions under the new Regional Development Incentives Act. The answer I received was that correspondence was exchanged only with the province of Alberta and the government of Alberta, and that with respect to the other provinces there was no correspondence.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
This seems to be a pretty strange way of running a government, a business or anything else. There is not a single scrap of correspondence dealing with the matter under consideration-a matter, incidentally, wherein it was a requirement of the legislation that there be consultation between the federal government and the province concerned before the federal government made a decision.
Subsequently, I obtained information regarding the proposals of the government of Alberta. This is information to which I felt I was entitled, and which I received. When I asked for information about the views of the federal government and the views of the other provinces across Canada, I was told that the details of such consultations were confidential. I suggest this is in conflict with the fact that I received information respecting one province. I suggest this sort of secrecy in carrying on the operations of the department in the long run will not stand the department in good stead in bringing these programs to the point of success.
I did obtain information subsequently when I asked for documents which would describe the criteria used by the department in selecting the designated areas across Canada for seven of the provinces. I obtained a table in each case entitled, "Economic growth measures for DBS regions". I examined each of these tables that I had requested for seven of the ten provinces, the other three being the Maritime provinces which were completely designated under this legislation. There was a series of tables. There was no indication given of the correlation among the various columns of figures in the tables. There was a table entitled "Income per capita 1966". This set of figures ranged, for example, in the province of British Columbia between 88 and 127. It is not quite clear to me what the 88 and 127 represent. It seems to be a pretty strange way of running a program, if this is the kind of information they use to establish their criteria.
There is a further set of figures dealing with population, comparing 1966 with 1961. It
Regional Development appears to be some sort of percentage change figure, but again this is not completely clear. The same is true with respect to a comparison of employment between 1968 and 1961, also income per capita comparison in 1964 to 1966 with 1961 to 1963.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, there is a composite change index. I found that this composite change index was apparently used as a starting point in establishing the regions across Canada. I have before me a map which I requested and which was supplied to me through the courtesy of the parliamentary secretary to the minister. It sets out the boundaries for these different DBS areas. I then took the figures supplied to me, the composite change index, and I found there were many cases-I could go into them in some detail if I had the time-which indicate that political influence was brought to bear in the final selection of designated areas across Canada. I hope to deal with some of these points on another occasion.
I wish to deal briefly with several other failures of the government in developing this legislation. The government failed to develop the growth centre concept in developing its program. It seems there is even conflict between the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) in their approach to this matter. I suggest, as well, there has been a give-away to the private sector of our economy. This has been carried on in the form of a shotgun approach; the government simply made grants to firms as they applied for them. This was done in quite a haphazard, scattergun manner. This policy involves a failure to develop any sort of an overallcomprehensive program for orderly development. At the same time, it represents a giveaway to the private sector of the economy.

However, the government holds no equity in these projects once it has

I suggest there has been gross failure by the government in allowing grants to be made to foreign-owned and foreign-controlled firms. There is a good deal of concern about this matter at the present time. Some ministers have expressed concern about it. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the opposition motion seeks to condemn the government for failure to co-ordinate its regional development policies under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion with other government activities, and for failure to make an appropriate reference to place this issue before the Standing Committee on Regional Development.
I suppose the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) who introduced this motion did so with sincerity. Nevertheless, I cannot easily imagine weaker wording for a motion designed to bring the activities of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion under review on an opposition day. Mr. Speaker, the co-ordination of the activities of government departments is precisely what this new department is all about. In April, 1969, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was established for the express purpose of co-ordinating government activities in the field of regional development.

The hon. member for St. John's East dealt in considerable detail with the shortcomings of various programs which have now been incorporated into the responsibility of this department. Surely, if there are shortcomings in the FRED program or the ADA program, for example, and if these shortcomings were related to a lack of co-ordination among government departments, as the motion indicates, the establishment of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion would put an end to these shortcomings, since it would bring all the various programs together.
I believe we should be careful not to underestimate the difficulty of bringing together programs as numerous and as various as the following:
1.	The Rural development branch of the Department of Fisheries and Forestry;
2.	Agricultural re-development (ARDA);
3.	The fund for regional economic development (FRED);
4.	The Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act (MMRA);
5.	The Area Development Agency (ADA);
6.	The Atlantic Development Board (ADB);
7.	The Canada Newstart Program;
8.	The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act (PFRA);
9.	The Cape Breton Development Corporation (Devco);
10.	The Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act.
I understand that the administration of these various programs has created the need for a new department with a staff of approximately 1,400 people. Indeed, in the department's annual report we find the final annual reports for these many programs as separate entities-the last occasion upon which they will be so listed.
Let us consider the degree of co-operation which exists among the various government departments. I have here an application for a development incentive grant under the Regional Development Incentives Act. Question No. 7 on this application form is: Will the operation produce wastes which would pollute air, water or soil? It seems clear to me that once the form has been filled out, the application must be directed to the attention of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, should the enterprise be likely to cause pollution to soil or water.
If it were likely to cause air pollution, reference would have to be made to the Depart-
February 3. 1970	COMMONS
ment of National Health and Welfare. I understand, too, that applications for incentive grants on the part of major industries are appraised by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to ensure as far as possible that these enterprises will be economically viable. Thereafter, assistance is made available as might be necessary in the field of trade or external sales.
It is interesting to note that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced the austerity program last summer involving cutbacks in the operations of many government departments, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was exempted from these measures because of the need to stimulate economic activity in the slow-growth areas. Though no one likes an austerity program, it may well be that this program, by bringing about a lack of funds for economic development in certain parts of the country, has increased the interest of industry in applying for the incentive grants available only to assist development in the slow-growth regions.
As one who comes from the constituency of Algoma, parts of which have been designated for many years, I welcome this increased interest shown by companies in establishing themselves in slow-growth areas. I am aware that there was a flood of applications for incentive grants during December, 1969. In the 1969 calendar year, 359 offers of incentive grants were made, resulting in 22,100 jobs. This compares with 98 approvals and 5,350 jobs expected for the year 1968. I believe this trend will continue and that the economic disparity which has existed for so long among various areas of Canada will be lessened in the years ahead.
Good co-ordination between federal government policies and departments does not always mean, however, that economic development will take place immediately. It should be remembered that many fields of governmental responsibility for development lie within provincial responsibility, and that unless the provincial government concerned is willing to co-operate with the federal government in its incentive program, little progress can be made.
For example, in my own constituency of Algoma, the town of Blind River has lost its only industry, the McFadden Lumber Company, which employed more than 300 people. The province of Ontario controls the forest limits which provide the wood fibre for this
