Mr. Speaker, when the regional development incentives bill was introduced to the House last June, we on this side welcomed the legislation as something we had been advocating for a good many years and to which we hoped the government would give first priority. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) pointed out at that time that we had been waiting a long time for this legislation, that the government had wasted too much time already in bringing it in, and that he hoped that now it had been introduced in the House it would be passed quickly and the government would move a little faster in bringing help to areas suffering regional disparity.
He also pointed out that because of the failure of the government to do anything for four or five years, a great deal of time had been lost in the Atlantic provinces and it behooved the government to move a little faster to make up for this lost time. He also expressed doubts that there had been any real change in government thinking and he wondered if they would actually move any faster once the legislation had been put through. The doubts that our leader expressed at that time were very real ones, and many people in the region, including myself, are beginning to question the government's good intentions in implementing this legislation.
Leading papers in the area have carried editorials on the subject, and in every case they are beginning to wonder if the government really means to take any immediate action to correct the problems of the region. Like most people in the Maritimes, I was quite happy to hear the minister's remarks in Saint John early in January, that his department was prepared to spend millions and millions of dollars in the Maritimes and that this could be done without adding anything to the inflationary pressures. But our enthusiasm likely will be tempered by native caution. Maritimers will, not unreasonably, await specific results before getting carried away by the minister's words, for his remarks are really nothing new.
We in that part of Canada have been saying for years that while there may be a
February 3, 1970

cost-push inflation in the rest of Canada, that is certainly not the problem in our area. Inflationary pressures may remain very high in the rest of Canada, but in the Atlantic area people are getting the worst of both worlds. We are already afflicted with high unemployment and low wages, and we are likely to be seriously hurt if the government in Ottawa does not tailor its financial policies to fit situations which exist in the depressed areas of the country.
It is little comfort to us in the Atlantic region to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) remark that he is prepared to take measures which might increase unemployment in the country up to 6 per cent or more. The Prime Minister recognizes that Ontario has been the chief cause of inflation, and he says that he is prepared to take stern measures to reduce these inflationary pressures.
What the Prime Minister does not seem to realize or care about is that we in the Atlantic area cannot wait much longer for this government to do something about unemployment. It is true that in New Brunswick we are hearing all sorts of vague rumours about great new developments to take place, but nobody says when. That will-o-the-wisp, the president of the New Brunswick Development Corporation, is chasing all over the world trying to entice industry to come to New Brunswick and only he knows what promises he is making. I have been told he does not even answer to his own Minister of Economic Growth. Our people are asking why there is this veil of secrecy. Public funds are being spent, and people are entitled to know what promises are being made. How could you expect the people of New Brunswick to have any confidence in a provincial government which could perpetrate the Fundy Chemical Park fiasco on them? Let the minister and his colleagues be frank and tell us what is going on.
The minister has given us some figures. He has told us about 17 grants that have been approved and how they are spread across the country. These figures in themselves suggest that the system of a single grant structure for all the slow-growth regions will not work. If a firm has a chance of receiving a grant in either Nova Scotia or Quebec, it is far more likely to choose Quebec as its location because it is so much closer to the main marketing and productive centres of Canada.
Regional Development

Professor T. N. Brewis in his book published last year and entitled "Regional Development Policies in Canada" noted that this problem of a uniform system of grants had been a problem of the area development incentives program. Under that program the underdeveloped areas of Ontario had been the obvious beneficiaries. There are also other indications that the regional development programs are failing to achieve their aims. The industries which are being attracted to the designated regions do not always come from the overcrowded, industrial centres of this country.
One example was brought to the attention of the House last December by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken). He referred to the Glaverbel Glass Company of Belgium which had sound intentions of locating a plant in Parry Sound but was suddenly attracted away to Quebec city by the regional incentives people. Parry Sound is hardly an area from which an industry should be lured away. Yet this is exactly the result of the programs being pursued by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. No wonder the minister is so anxious to keep quiet about the activities of his department.
So far I have dealt with what might be called incidents of failure in the regional development program. But a far more serious consequence than these incidents has been the gross failure of this government to co-ordinate its other policies with its regional development policies. There are three prime examples of the government's flagrant disregard for regional development in the over-all policies, namely, the proposals of the white paper on taxation, the anti-inflationary policies of the government, and the austerity program in government spending.
The white paper hits hard at small business-despite the protest of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson)-which is the type of business most commonly found in the slow-growth areas. It proposes to remove the special, lower tax rate for small businesses and thus raise their tax bill and reduce their ability to plough earnings back into the business. Owners of small publicly-traded businesses will have difficulty maintaining ownership when faced with a tax bill every five years for the capital gains on the stock they hold in their companies. Farmers, too, will be hit by the new tax proposals. Capital gains taxing of their sales of livestock and equipment, and

February 3, 1970
Regional Development
the removal of tax concessions previously granted to farm co-operatives, will certainly cut into farm income.
The government also has unfavourable changes in store for the extractive industries. In other words, the tax paper manages to strike at the three staples of the slow growth areas: small business, farming, and extraction. Is this an indication of the government's sincerity about improving regional economies?
Another example is the anti-inflationary measures taken by this government. The Prime Minister says his government will fight inflation even if the national unemployment rate goes as high as 6 per cent. But the unemployment rate in Quebec is already 7 per cent; in the Atlantic provinces it is already 7.4 per cent, while the national rate is 4.8 per cent. If the national rate is allowed to go to 6 per cent, these high unemployment areas will be hit much harder. C. R. McFadden, head of the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, estimates that unemployment in the Maritimes could go as high as 10 per cent. In other words, the government is quite prepared to let the slow-growth areas of the country underwrite the cost of restoring price stability.
The spending of the government under its program of austerity is equally lopsided. With cries of "Economy" and "Let's tighten our belts" the government has cut back spending on the Newstart program and has frozen hiring for the Cape Breton Development Corporation. At the same time, it feels no pangs of conscience about spending $27 million for a new defence headquarters in Ottawa.
In fact, the spending of the Department of Public Works in general is an instructive case. Take, for example, the department's release concerning contracts let during the month of November. In all the areas which the government did not single out in its budget for restraints on capital spending, Public Works awarded contracts with a total value of $2,383,781. In Toronto alone, its contracts were worth nearly three times as much. In Ottawa, its contracts were worth nearly ten times as much, and construction worth $50 million more is planned for Ottawa beginning this summer.
The government is preaching restraint for the weaker areas of the economy while pumping money into the centres of inflation, and this despite the minister's statement in Saint John early last month that the government could spend "millions and millions of

dollars in the Maritimes without adding anything to inflationary pressures". Of course, he did not say anything about the rest of the country-I admit that-but it hardly ties in with the government's war against inflation to spend millions of dollars in inflationary areas and not in the depressed areas.
To summarize my main points, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand) has created great anxiety in those of us who are interested in regional development by his persistent refusal to remove the secrecy which surrounds the operations of his department. Such secrecy, along with the small bits of information which have managed to leak out about the department's performance, lead us to believe that the program is foundering badly.
No matter how well the department's own programs were doing, they could not possibly compensate for the department's utter failure to fulfil its role in co-ordinating other government programs with regional impact. The fiscal and monetary policies of the present government are such as to wipe out entirely any good which might have been done under the regional development program.
Almost no one disagrees with the aims of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. If the minister would only re-open the channels for discussion of his policies, he might find that he has gained valuable allies for the struggles in which he is obviously engaged with other members of the cabinet.

Have we actually the right to blame the government? Surely if we study all the aspects of the problem, we can certainly do so, because, in everything, there is always some good and some bad, and men are not more perfect than the laws that they enact.
The new department had in mind, I think, a comprehensive project, and it urges all groups: provincial governments, municipalities, companies, industrialists, to come and co-operate with a view to reducing unemployment across Canada.
If the government is to be blamed in some instances, we also have to examine our own conscience, since that question is of the utmost interest to us. We must ask ourselves whether we have done our duty and have informed the population on the aims of the department.
The minister, in the introduction to the report of his department for the year 1968-69, stated the following, and I quote:
The first phase in the establishment of the new department was dealing with the re-grouping under the authority of a single minister of ail the federal organizations and programs devoted to regional development and social progress. The
Regional Development
oldest of those programs dated back to 1935, but most of them had been initiated since 1960; each was designed to settle what was originally considered distinct and isolated cases-
As a matter of fact, a few years ago, when the famous ARDA program was introduced, I had the opportunity to rise in the House and to congratulate the then Minister of Forestry. I drew to his attention in particular the fact that, thanks to the ARDA program, many blueberry operations had been set up in my region. We got grants totalling more than $3 million to that effect. I then told the minister that he was making a big mistake by setting up those blueberry operations.
Six or seven years later, it turned out that I had been right. The blueberry fields have become public places where pickers are fighting for the blueberries. Once everything had been levelled down, I told him: You should not have caused all those trees to be chopped down, because you should know that blueberries grow in the woods with trees a necessary protection.
Well, what is being done now? Just a return to what I recommended six or seven years ago. I quote from a November 1969 newspaper:
Parcels of land will be distributed to the pickers.
So the blueberry fields which had almost been regionalized are going to be returned to the owners.
I believed it was a mistake at the time and I had censored the government for thus venturing into areas it was not too familiar with. I had precisely told the minister that he knew nothing about blueberry operations. This was no fault of his, but he should have heeded my advice.
Today, because of these failures, blueberry production has considerably decreased. However the new arrangements should result in correcting these mistakes.
This organization has been established recently, as I said a moment ago. Its aim is to centralize all efforts in an attempt to solve the problem as a whole.
If we really want to solve it, co-operation is essential on the part of the provinces, companies and industrialists.
The Quebec government has certainly understood the aims of this department, since in September 1969 a newspaper stated that it intended to invest $50 million in the program for financial assistance to primary industries.

February 3, 1970
Regional Development
Reading this article, I understood immediately that the province of Quebec was aware of the part it had to play, since it allocated funds for joint programs which the Department of Regional Economic Expansion will help to put into effect in each of the regions.
As far as my riding is concerned, much work has been done. In fact, we have benefit-ted from the planning mission as well as from the REC which is doing an excellent job in determining means to promote industry, agriculture and tourism.
We have obtained an excellent report of some 450 pages which is full of valuable information. On reading that report, some deficiencies are discovered, even in my area. Indeed, some authorities, such as reeves, have violently criticized it. In my opinion, it has given too much importance to the Upper Saguenay area in comparison with others, namely the Lake St. John and Roberval areas.
Apparently, all the industry has been centered in the Upper Saguenay, while the Lake St. John area becomes an experimental farm. In fact, it is considered as being mainly a farming district, while the best farm lands happen to be in the Roberval area where the future of forestry operations looks very promising.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
It will probably be necessary to retimber the present lands in order to start a forest development.
If one of our distinguished citizens, a reeve, expressed straightforwardly his opinions on that matter, he was sometimes right. If it had been arranged to have the study made by people of the area, I think the results would have been different.
Anyway I do not wish to destroy everything that has been done because there has been some progress. What has been achieved is surely not useless since it has already given rise to discussions and certainly it has helped the minister realize that the people of the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean area are not only awakening but want to study the problems and get out of the present dead-lock.
We have already seen some results in our area, since we have received a grant for one of our most prosperous industries, one that manufactures machinery used in forestry, such as motor chain-saws and, in my opinion, this is quite an achievement. We hope this assistance will be continued, in order that

other similar industries will contribute to the recovery of our economy which is not based entirely on the forest industry because the people there also go in for farming. We also hope that in this field we will be able some day to note some progress.
We have also a very interesting project in St.-Felicien and there is no need for me to cross the t's, as the Minister knows what I am alluding to. Besides, I contacted him on that subject and I am sure that the Minister will do what he can so that the studies about St.-Felicien be carried out as soon as possible, because the region needs it. This industry would create 2,000 or 2,500 jobs. I think that it is a constructive project and I feel sure that the Minister is very much interested in it.
Besides, I received the other day from the city of Roberval-the Minister must have got one too-a copy of the memorandum which it submitted to the economic mission-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-FAILURE TO CO-ORDINATE REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT POLICIES AND TO REFER ISSUE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I was talking to the leader of the House, my hon. friend from Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald), and he expressed concern about some of the comments which had been made in connection with the tardiness of the regional development committee in convening again after the fall recess.
As the chairman of that committee, and in an effort to be fair and objective, I feel that with all due respect to members of the House, and in answer to their complaints that they have been left in the dark about what the committee and the department have been doing, I should review what the committee has done over the past 18 months.
As many members know, this was a new committee, one made up of people here for the first time and who were not familiar with committee procedure. The committee encountered a further handicap in that it was immediately presented with the estimates of two government departments which were being phased out. In studying these estimates and listening to hon. members such as the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Maclnnis) and the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir), we probably heard more about coal mines and found out more on the subject of coal and steel than we ever realized we did not know. As we pro-
February 3, 1970

gressed through the Maritimes and into the west we picked up an idea of just what the government had been trying to establish through the fragmented departmental programs and the ARDA development plan. We had a taste of what might be accomplished by the new department which was being instituted.
Having made progress through the estimates, we decided at the steering committee meetings that we would go to the west and investigate on site the FRED, ARDA and Newstart programs. These were, of course, older programs and it was easier to judge how they were accomplishing the ends which the departments had sought to achieve. Nevertheless, the committee kept in mind the eloquent plea from Bell Island. It decided, and fully intended, to go to Newfoundland and the Maritimes to look into the problems of transportation which we knew existed there. However, we decided to go west first.
I recall, as we got to Prince Albert, our first stop, the sense of frustration which I felt. It is curious that the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) should have opened his remarks by talking about frustration. Members of the opposition refer to their frustration when they look across to the government benches. I will always remember the frustration I experienced, because I understood what those kids must have felt when they got to the airport, having driven 80 or 100 miles to see that bright young member of the committee, the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville, and found that after all he was not with us. I sensed their frustration and I, too, was frustrated. I knew that this young member's mind was probably filled with his marriage and his forthcoming nuptials, and that he just could not be with us. I am sure he, too, was frustrated-not with his marriage, of course, but with his inability to be present at that time.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Here we have different frustrations and they probably all revert back basically to the people. You cannot think of government; you must think of the people. This was true of our committee work. I was impressed, and I know members of the committee were, with Newstart. The people, particularly those from Newfoundland, had never seen anything like it. As a matter of fact, they had never had a program like this on the island. We found that ARDA programs had worked wonders.
Regional Development
After returning to Ottawa with the experience we gained in the west, we knew what we intended to do. We were prepared to go to the east, study the existing programs there and make recommendations as to how they could be improved. The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) generously suggested, when we got back and were confronted with the bill to establish the Regional Development Incentives Act, that we did not have much choice. If we postponed the committee study of this bill and decided to go east, the whole program would have been put off for six or nine momhs because of the summer break; we probably would not be having this debate tonight because we would just be considering the first stage of the measure.
The committee in its enthusiasm for this measure, and with its tremendous responsibility-I cannot praise the members too highly- studied the bill and returned it to this House in time to pass it by the end of June in order that the new department could commence with the program hon. members have been discussing tonight. Following this we adjourned for the summer.
There was some discussion about going to Newfoundland and the Maritimes even at that time. I would have been very happy to go there even though it might have been too early for tuna fishing. I still think it would have been a good trip. But hon. members were tired, they had worked hard during the spring, and the consensus was that it would be better if we waited until the fall.
Had we gone to the east in the summer, a double load would have fallen upon the shoulders of hon. members. Had we gone there and presented ourselves as the great white hope, if you will, or the seviour to the people suffering regional disparity, we might have raised their hopes for no real reason, because we were going just to look. We were not prepared immediately to say we intended to enter into constructive programs. In any event, it was decided to put off that trip.
During the summer numerous letters were exchanged, there were telephone calls and there was a meeting. Often the 264 members of this chamber have a hard time reaching agreement. I realize that the "famous five" who were attempting to plan the Newfoundland trip were probably experiencing difficulty in reaching agreement on priority and the areas the committee should visit. I have no direct knowledge of this, but knowing their enthusiasm, and with my interest in their

February 3, 1970
Regional Development
problems, I am sure if there had been a meeting of minds we would have done something before October or November.
I do not wish to ingratiate myself with the minister, and certainly I am not the type to ingratiate myself with the government. However, I take complete responsibility for the committee not being reconvened in December. The House Leader spoke to me about this matter. In fact, he advised the committees branch that we should reconvene. Perhaps I did not have the authority, but after talking to the members of the committee I decided there was no real purpose in reconvening and that nothing of significance could be accomplished if we did reconvene in December.
The members of this committee are young and enthusiastic. They are not the type of committee members who want to sit in committee just for the sake of doing something. There were other committees sitting in December which demanded much of hon. members' time. On that basis, I advised the House Leaders that we would be better advised to wait until we had the first full year's estimates of the department before the committee for study.
Let me say without any malice, and not as a snide remark, that opposition members have the advantage of the research people which this government has provided. They are a great deal better off than we, for this reason. If they have had any spare time during the time the House has been sitting, I hope they have used their research people to prepare themselves for the committee's study of the estimates. I hope when this study commences they will present many constructive ideas. Let them tear the estimates apart, without knocking them just for the sake of knocking them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-FAILURE TO CO-ORDINATE REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT POLICIES AND TO REFER ISSUE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious that the government which was elected in 1968 intended that the Department of Regional Development should be the keystone in the so-called just society. This afternoon the latest report from the department came into my hands. I notice that the second paragraph on page 1 confirms this viewpoint. It says, with reference to the establishment of this department:
The announcement stemmed from the Prime Minister's previously declared policy of making regional development a matter of top priority for the government.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I think it will be equally obvious from the worth-while debate that has taken place today that, while the government might have intended to make the Department of Regional Economic Development the cornerstone of the implementation of the just society, it has fallen far short of the mark with respect to implementation. Notwithstanding the large amount of propaganda, as demonstrated by the many press releases that have been issued, this program unfortunately has not yet got off the ground. In fact, I would think the amount of attention that has been paid in speeches and press releases to this subject has aggravated a situation which is inherent in the Canadian body politic, that is, the prob-
(Mr. Morison.]
February 3, 1970

February 3, 1970
Regional Development
than any other in binding this nation from sea to sea.
I think everybody who understands the problems of Canadian confederation will agree with that. Under this new department the minister has that opportunity. Solving regional economic disparity is not an easy task because our climatic and geographic conditions aggravate the problem. For years Ottawa stayed clear of its obligation in this regard and we did not advance very much on the original national policy that first brought Canada together. Nothing happened really until the late 1950s.
Much can be done through policy decisions of this government. The minister said during the course of his speech that some areas are affected by deflation and others inflation. I wish he would communicate this information to his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), because one of the reasons for the misunderstanding concerning the government's approach to regional disparity is the unequal application of the austerity program.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The austeri'y program has slowed down or cancelled programs that were actually on the drawing board. This applies particularly to some projects under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, and I would say this situation is more apparent in western Canada than in any other operation that the federal government might carry out. It offsets all the propaganda and the press reports about increasing job opportunities.
As a result of the growing problems in the west, the Premier of Manitoba visited Ottawa not long ago to bring some of these difficulties to the attention of the minister and a few of his colleagues. I would point out that the provinces actually were ahead of Ottawa in coming to grips with special regional, economic incentives which have become necessary in our post-World War II economy. Manitoba introduced a dynamic program in the late 1950s. In close co-operation with Ottawa it introduced power development programs such as the Shellmouth Dam project which has been in progress all this time and will be completed this year, the erection of vocational schools, the Winnipeg floodway, and so forth.
Following his talks in Ottawa, the Premier of Manitoba was interviewed by the Winnipeg Free Press. In a red headline, almost as large as those that used to be created by the deputy minister, it stated, "Schreyer Unsatisfied with Talks", with a subheading "Federal
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
Piecemeal Approach Disappoints Manitoba Premier." This is why the west is hopping mad. The premier said that no matter how hard Manitoba pressed its counterparts in the federal cabinet, it could get no clear picture of the federal funds that would be available to Manitoba through the Department of Economic Regional Expansion.
To use a quotation I picked up just this evening from the Ottawa Journal, Mr. Speaker, I say that the government has been sounding the bugle long enough concerning the success of its programs. Now it must teach the bugler to play "Charge!" and get to the essence of the problems. If no funds are available from Ottawa, no programs will be implemented at the provincial level.
Even though this motion is not coming to a vote, I hope that everything said in the chamber today will not be lost on the minister. Our approach is positive. We have tried to bring to his attention some of the difficulties in various parts of Canada. I hope he has listened to what members have said about the growing disenchantment of the west, and that he will seize his responsibilities as leader of this new department and see that the new national development program, which the Winnipeg Free Press used to talk about, will be implemented in fact as well as in propaganda.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-FAILURE TO CO-ORDINATE REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT POLICIES AND TO REFER ISSUE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to add a few words after hearing some members of the opposition. This motion is to say the least untimely under the circumstances.
I think that the government is the least to blame when it comes to restructuring all its activities in order to stop economic disparities.
Some members of the opposition want, as a matter of fact, a little childishly, to force the government to solve within less than a year problems which have always existed. In my opinion they just want, as the previous speaker said, to give rise to hate among the people instead of appealing to their reason.
If we upbraid the Department of Regional Economic Expansion for inaction and question the implications of the legislation, namely those of Bill C-202, passed on June 27, 1969, that is barely six months ago, this in no way settles the economic problems of this country, nor suppresses the regional economic disparities. Above all, this shows a lack of
February 3, 1970

understanding of the means of action at the government's disposal.
Regional disparities exist and they would tend to increase at the expense of the future well-being of our citizens in the absence of governmental intervention. Then, how should we behave? There will never be efficient governmental action without concurrent initiative on the part of private citizens and private enterprise.
Unless we create basic structures designed to urge the private citizens or private enterprise to act, and unless some economic controls are imposed, only initiative and incentives will generate action.
Bill C-202 which was passed by the House last June deals with industrial incentives required for developing depressed regions. Within a very short period and thanks to their ini'ia'ive, the people will manage to eliminate these regional disparities.
I represent an economically underprivileged region. Before introducing Bill C-202, the department acted with wisdom and clearsightedness by selecting the disadvantaged regions; earlier, this was rather like a strait-jacket which effec'ively prevented the government from acting.
What is more desirable yet is coordination. It already exists within the department, but it must also exist within provincial government and municipalities. The latter claim that they do not have the necessary financial means to honorably discharge their duties, but they have however the first say insofar as the development of the territory is concerned. Because of the very large number of municipalities, such aclion de'eriorates and is often lacking in co-ordination and planning.
But at the provincial level, industrial incentives work together wi'h economic wealth, thus creating a force which goes against solutions likely to eliminate regional disparities.
If we are able to take advantage of natural means of action, namely natural resources, the implementation of Bill C-202 and the action of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand), wi'h the help of personal initiative and co-ordination at all government levels, will bring, I submit, concrete results.
In spite of what certain members may think, we are at the present time faced with the serious problem of unemployment. We hope that the legislations passed by this
Regional Development
government will enable us to solve partly the problem of unemployment, as well as the one not less serious, concerning regional disparities.
Instead of blaming the government which is setting itself to a mammoth task, I suggest it would be better to bring forward constructive suggestions.
I shall conclude my remarks by saying that the measures adopted by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and by the agencies it has set up, are quite efficient, and that the government will attain its objectives.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-FAILURE TO CO-ORDINATE REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT POLICIES AND TO REFER ISSUE TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel I have been "had" without the benefit of osculation. I am particularly interested in this bill because it affects the part of Canada that I come from, where not too much is being done. The minister would deserve a great deal more credit if he would agree to set up a committee to make reports, instead of leaving that to his parliamentary secretary. One of the problems of his department is that he has always left things to somebody else. He has a background of national attachment in his former occupation. I had a long period of international attachment, and now I have become a strong nationalist and he a strong provincialist.
All afternoon I have heard complaints from the maritimers; but if anything has been done anywhere, that is the place. I would like to hear some maritimers ask the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to put money into the heavy water plant which was to bring so many benefits to the province of Nova Scotia. Surely they cannot afford to tie up $100 million in this project. It was built on federal advice, and it is up to the federal government to salvage it. The people of the Mariiimes cannot afford to lose their investment in the project. The minister should look into the whole matter before they lose any more money.
Mr. Speaker, I recommend to the minister the documents of the mid-Canada corridor concept put out by Acres Research. I am well aware of the merits of this document as well as its weaknesses. As a socialist I have no intention of turning over all of the mid-Canada corridor for private enterprise to exploit, but they have indicated the resources that are available, the massive expenditure involved and the rewards of such develop-

February 3, 1970
Regional Development
ment. This will never happen under this minister, for the simple reason that the provinces will not allow the federal government to have full control of the area unless the federal government states how much it is willing to spend.
It seems that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) has considered this kind of project in relation to northern development because he has been interested in the development of a concept where business and government get together and evolve the total concept of a given area. The time has come for us to look forward. Shared-cost programs have failed and the people will not again become excited about ARDA, FRED or any similar projects.
If the federal government has a role, it is to look at the total concept of what can be done and set about doing it in an orderly fashion. As long as the federal government is willing to put up the money, the provinces will not throw any roadblocks in the way. I am sick and tired of all this bickering back and forth about what areas are to be designated. The federal government has to make the decision. The provinces are willing to let them put up the money, but they want the say in how the projects are run.
This program is not bringing new industry into my area, where resources are plentiful. We have put out money for a sawmill to be built or expanded, for a plywood factory or some other factory that was proposed for the area. I have no quarrel with the priority given to this program by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), but let us look at it on a national basis. I have listened with great patience all afternoon to complaints about projects in individual areas. Surely, in the national Parliament we are interested in a national concept. We know that the area of Canada which is not developed is the mid-Canada corridor, and we know that industry from the Golden Horseshoe will not go into that area unless it is provided with great incentives. Such incentives need not necessarily be monetary; they may have relation to the total concept of what can be done in the area. It is here that the government should be giving leadership to industry.
I hope that before the committee meets the minister will state what is to be done about the one project that has cost the Maritimes more money than any other and which will go down the drain unless the federal government gives assistance. I hope he suggests that certain things be done in conjunction with

Atomic Energy so that at least that problem will be solved to the satisfaction of all Canadians.
The concept of regional development, Mr. Speaker, is national, not provincial and not parochial. I suggest we get on with the national concept of regional development.

subsubtopic: TRANSPORT-COAL-APPLICATION BY GREAT NORTHERN AND KOOTENAY ELK RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 3 I directed the following question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson), as recorded at page 1554 of Hansard:
Has the Canadian Transport Commission received an application from the Great Northern Railway Company and the Kootenay Elk Railway Company for permission to build lines into the United States and back into Canada at the Pacific coast for the purpose of carrying coal to the Pacific coast via the United States?
This question is of vital importance to the economy of British Columbia and to Canada in general. I welcome the opportunity to raise it at this time so that further information and facts on the situation can be placed on the record. Perhaps the minister will give the House tonight some information on both these applications and the hearings which I understand are now under way.
Since raising my question in the House there have been several articles in the various news media from information supplied by Crows Nest Industries Limited, one of the applicants interested in building a rail link to the United States and shipping Canadian coal via United States railway lines. This company is trying to tell the Canadian public that CPR lacks the carrying capacity to meet the
February 3, 1970	COMMONS
demands of the Japanese steel industry for Canadian coal. It indicates that the freight rates asked by CPR are higher than the company can afford to pay.
Last year a similar controversy took place when the Kaiser Coal Company advocated the shipping of Canadian coal via the Great Northern Railway to Roberts Bank. At that time I thought this matter had been settled. The CPR apparently negotiated an acceptable freight rate of $3.50 per long ton of coal for a 15-year period. I understand that since that time it has added another contract for two million tons annually at the same rate.
However, the charge that CPR lines cannot handle the coal which will be mined in East Kootenay is a disturbing one and, in my opinion, is not based on any factual evidence which Crows Nest Industries Limited can produce. I am opposed to the shipment of Canadian resources over United States railway lines if we can possibly ship the material via an all-Canadian route. Any time we use our transportation systems in Canada, we are providing more jobs for Canadians and we are also adding, as in the case of this huge coal contract, many millions of dollars annually to the Canadian economy.
There are other advantages to shipping by an all-Canadian route which might not be readily discernible to the general Canadian public. One advantage is the employment which the supplying of the equipment gives to Canadians in many parts of our country. For example, the coal cars are built in the Hawker-Siddeley plant in Nova Scotia; steel for these cars comes from Hamilton; the locomotives are built in Montreal; the steel rails come from Algoma Steel at Sault Ste. Marie; the wooden ties for the track come from various parts of Canada; workmen on trains come from our own railway unions. Their money, plus the freight rates, accrues to individuals and companies within Canada. It is worth millions of dollars to our economy.
Here is an estimate of the Canadian labour income which results from coal traffic moved on Canadian lines. From the Kootenay area of B.C. to the West Coast, for each one million long tons of coal moved annually there is a return of about $1.2 million annually. This means an annual outlay of labour income from the present five million tons of coal being moved of about $6 million. This labour income represents wages, salaries and related railway employee benefits. There is little enough return to the Canadian economy through the development of this resource. We
DEBATES	3179
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion cannot afford to lose the jobs and the purchasing power involved by shipping coal by way of the United States.
At present the CPR has two contracts for hauling coal. One contract is for 15 years at three million tons per year. The second contract is for three years at two million tons per year. During the period in which it will be hauling five million tons per year they plan to use two trains per day with 88 cars in each. On April 1, 1972, the Fording Coal Company plans to ship another three million tons per year in addition to the figures I have given. This will require another 105-car train.
I am surprised that Crow's Nest Industries Limited has applied to build a connecting link with the Great Northern Railway in the United States. To my knowledge, this company does not yet have a buyer for any of its coal. This fact alone should void its present application. In my opinion, its charge that CPR does not have the carrying capacity to handle all the coal in the Fernie area is also unfounded. From information I have been able to obtain it would appear that CPR has ordered 578 cars, 37 diesel locomotives and 5 robot cars which will be sufficient to handle the contracts they now hold. Other equipment can be added as required. I understand the main CPR line from Calgary to Vancouver averages 7 trains per day in each direction. Sometimes there is a peak of ten trains per day, if there is a rush on wheat, potash and coal at the same time.
In 1968 a centralized traffic control system on this line was completed. It can now handle a minimum of one train an hour in each direction. Taking the present peak of 10 trains per day, it means that another 14 trains, minimum, per day could travel this route. I am informed that the present 3 million tons yearly contract requires only one train per day which consists of 105 cars. This is based on 345 days per year. A 20-day period in the year should cover any line interruptions or breakdown at the mine or shipping port. Trains can be made longer if needed and can go to a maximum of 115 cars. These longer trains would still fit the siding capacities and the facilities at both ends, because the loading and unloading has been designed to handle 150 cars if needed, together with the motor power. This additional available capacity of 10 cars per train would add a further safety factor as far as delays and interruptions are concerned.

In addition, we have an alternate route over the Kettle Valley line which serves my own constituency. There are also several interchanges where Canadian Pacific Railway trains can transfer to Canadian National Railways' tracks in the event of trouble. There is even an interchange near Grand Forks, British Columbia, where trains could transfer to the Great Northern if a real and lengthy emergency occurred.
The picture is clear to me, Mr. Speaker. I feel that CPR has the equipment or can obtain it. It has the line capacity. It has Canadian workmen using mostly Canadian-produced equipment. If CPR is anywhere near competitive in freight rates, and apparently it is, there should be no hesitation in the Canadian government insisting that these Canadian resources should be hauled to Canadian ports via an all-Canadian route.

The Canadian Transport Commission advises as follows with respect to the status of applications received in the matter of the Kootenay & Elk Railway Company. The Railway Transport Committee of the commission received on November 28, 1969, the following applications:
1.	Application under section 255 and other applicable sections of the Railway Act to join the proposed line of the Kootenay & Elk Company with the line of Great Northern Railway Company at or near the border between British Columbia and the state of Montana, near Rooseville West.
2.	An application under section 255 of the Railway Act to cross the railway of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company near Hosmer in British Columbia, with the proposed line of Kootenay & Elk Railway.
3.	An application under the Crowsnest Pass Agreement, chapter 5 of the Statutes of Canada, 1896-97, for running rights over the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company between Natal and Elko in the province of British Columbia.
Applications two and three are said to be alternative applications and the applicant

states that if its application for running rights under the Crowsnest Pass Agreement is granted, the application to cross the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's line north of Hosmer will be withdrawn. subsubtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-REPRESENTATIONS BY DIABETIC ASSOCIATION RESPECTING CYCLAMATE BAN-AVAILABILITY OF SUBSTITUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in bringing forth this matter this evening was prompted by the questions I posed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) a few days ago concerning the recently announced ban on cyclamates and the resultant hardships created as a result in the dietary planning of those afflicted with diabetes.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The questions, as recorded in Hansard at page 2969, were as follows:
In view of the recent ban on cyclamates and subsequent representations made to the minister by the Canadian Diabetic Association indicating that as a result severe hardship has been imposed upon those inflicted with diabetes, is any consideration being given to making available a substitute in order that diabetics may acquire some relief?
February 3, 1970	COMMONS
To which the minister answered: "Yes, Mr. Speaker." The exchange continued:
In the meantime, is the minister giving any consideration to permitting the use of controlled amounts of cyclamates by those afflicted with diabetes?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-REPRESENTATIONS BY DIABETIC ASSOCIATION RESPECTING CYCLAMATE BAN-AVAILABILITY OF SUBSTITUTE
speechtext:
Depending on what is meant by controlled, yes, Mr. Speaker.
I had hoped to extract more detail than that, Mr. Speaker; frankly, I found the minister's answer somewhat vague. I trust that tonight the House and the country will be given an opportunity to learn exactly what steps are being taken to overcome the confusion which presently faces doctors and patients who are finding difficulty controlling their diets following the ban.
I realize that the minister is not able to be present this evening, but I am sure his parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz), himself a medical practitioner, can provide us with some of the details.
According to a newsletter issued on October 21 by the department, dietetic canned fruit containing cyclamates is to be banned on September 1, 1970. I am told that wholesalers in many areas have informed retailers, distributors and hospitals that they will no longer be able to supply these canned fruits after February 1. I am advised that this raises a difficult problem for diabetics in formulating a proper diet, particularly in areas where fresh fruits are not always readily available.
I am not a medical man, so, with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote from a letter which I received from a medical doctor who has some misgivings about the way in which the question of cyclamates is at present being handled. He writes:
I have found that statements made concerning cyclamates have been very confusing to the many diabetic patients that I have to see. The one thing which I think might help would be the issuing of some statement as to the amount of cyclamates which could safely be taken each day. I am also wondering if it would be possible to have the amount of cyclamates present in the various diabetic foods stated clearly on the food labels. I think if this information were available it might not be necessary to take these foods off the market; I believe that such action is likely to impose real hardship on the many diabetics who attempt to keep good control of their disease.
The letter goes on to say:
I also wonder whether the labels on the diet foods for diabetics could be printed so they would show the food exchange value. All diabetics understand how to use these food exchanges which
DEBATES	3181
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion are listed in the meal planning booklet put out by the Canadian Diabetic Association.
Again referring to the newsletter of October 21, issued by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the following is stated: -we have no scientific evidence at this point to indicate that cyclamates have caused cancer or any other harmful effects in humans.
The newsletter also states that while there was evidence of cancer in rats, it was prevalent after extremely high dosage, 50 times higher than that accepted as that being safe for adults as prescribed by the World Health Organization. The newsletter goes on to say on behalf of the minister:
Let me repeat and emphasize the fact that there is no evidence that cyclamates have caused cancer or any other disease in humans.
The newsletter states further:
Four days ago, however, new evidence appeared that cyclamates produced tumours when fed to rats-at very high levels for long periods of time.
Further on it says that no tumours developed in rats given cyclamates at doses equivalent on a body-weight basis to that of 200 bottles of soft drinks per day throughout the lifetime of a 150-pound man. The newsletter continues:
It is obvious, therefore, that the danger to humans from cyclamates is undoubtedly very small.
I am sure most Canadians have no objection to the banning of cyclamates if sufficient evidence can be produced that the product is potentially capable of producing harmful side-effects. However, if harmful effects have not occurred until exorbitant amounts are consumed and this seems to be backed by many members of the medical profession they would be acceptable.
Perhaps if a standard could be issued dealing with safe amounts of cyclamates or the tolerant factor, indicating the amount which could be consumed without causing harmful effects, this would go a long way in assisting those who must practice dietary control. It is also my understanding that the United States has modified the ban on cyclamates and permits the sale of foods containing cyclamates, but it will maintain its ban in respect of beverages. I think this fact does have significance, and I hope the minister will undertake to take steps so that diabetics in Canada may once again look forward to leading normal lives.

The minister is also well aware of the problems of diabetics in Canada. Officers of the Food and Drugs Directorate have had discussions with the Dietetic Counselling Commission of the Canadian Diabetic Association on the subject of cyclamates. They have also discussed the matter in some detail with representatives of the various industry groups concerned.
As a result of these latter discussions we know that it is possible to produce dietetic beverages, spreads and foods, without the use of cyclamates. This is accomplished by modifying the formulas and the use of permitted flavours along with a sweetening agent
DEBATES	February 3, 1970
known as saccharin. The use of these new foods should permit diabetics to have a suitable variety of diet without running the risk of using cyclamates.
I would also remind the hon. member that my minister has never at any time questioned the need of diabetics for sweetening preparations for home use. These products will continue to be available under special labelling, the details of which have not yet been fully determined. It is anticipated, however, that their labels would carry a warning to the effect that they should be used only on the advice of a physician. With these measures being taken, my minister believes that Canadian diabetics should have no cause for concern over the ban of cyclamates in special dietary foods.
